**The answer.** **21-F11 is WITHDRAWN. I was wrong.** `score mate 0` on a checkmated root is the
correct UCI score, not a fault: `score mate <y>` means "mate in y moves for the side to move", so
`y = 0` is "already mated". A mated side has no move to play, so `bestmove 0000` is right too.
Nothing to repair, and nobody should spend time on it.

**How sure.** High, and it is measured rather than asserted: the engine's own scale is
consistent across three roots whose truth python-chess establishes.

| build | case | python truth | bestmove | score | matches convention |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| base | side to move is checkmated | checkmate | `0000` | `mate 0` | yes |
| base | side to move can mate in 1 | can mate in 1 | `e1e8` | `mate 1` | yes |
| base | side to move is stalemated | stalemate | `0000` | `cp 0` | yes |
| pc | side to move is checkmated | checkmate | `0000` | `mate 0` | yes |
| pc | side to move can mate in 1 | can mate in 1 | `e1e8` | `mate 1` | yes |
| pc | side to move is stalemated | stalemate | `0000` | `cp 0` | yes |

If `mate 0` were a broken scale, `mate 1` would not come out right on the same build in the
same run. Both are right, so the scale is sound.

## How I got it wrong

In `job16` I saw `score mate 0` on a checkmated root, checked only that python-chess agrees the
position is checkmate, and concluded the score must be wrong because "a mated side should report
a loss". That reasoning inverted the convention: `mate N` in UCI is relative to the SIDE TO MOVE,
so being mated now is `mate 0`, not `mate -N`. I did not test a positive mate score in the same
run, which would have shown me the scale at once. That is the check I have now done.

This is the second time in this session that my own control caught me (the first was the
fullmove patch that wrongly accepted `-1`). Both are on the record rather than quietly fixed.

1. **The bail path and its guards:** `search.cpp:2250-2271`. Guards are `!legal.empty()` (`:2251`),
   `board.is_repetition()` (`:2251` → `board.cpp:1224-1233`), `board.halfmove_clock() >= 100` (`:2251`),
   `board.is_insufficient_material()` (`:2252` → `board.cpp:1250-1257`), `root_candidates.empty()` (`:2253`,
   the `searchmoves` arm), and `DrawJitter > 0` (`:2256`, a re-score, not a selector).
2. **What it publishes and why:** `result.best_move = root_candidates.front()` (`:2265`) with
   `result.nodes = total_nodes()` (`:2266`) = 0. `root_candidates` is a generator-order copy made at `:2203-2209`,
   and no ordering stage has run, because ordering in this engine is lazy inside `MovePicker::pick_best()`
   (`:817-863`) which the branch never reaches. Verified: `go perft 1`'s first move equals the bail's `bestmove` on
   6 of 6 bailing cells. The intended contract is "terminal root: answer the protocol without searching"
   (`:2250` comment; asserted by `tests_r3fu_17/reused_searcher.cpp:71-76` and
   `tests_r3_13/quiet_extinction.cpp:99-114`); `best_move` carries a placeholder there, with no field in
   `SearchInfo` (`include/forge/search.hpp:58-69`) marking it as unchosen.
3. **Guard vs ordering:** the guard is **before** the ID loop (`:2253` vs `:2391`) and before any ordering, but
   **after** legal-move generation (`:2202`). That is why a bailing cell returns the generator index 0 while a
   searching cell returns picker index 5.

## The fault, in one sentence

On the base tree, a root with halfmove counter **≥ 100** is declared drawn **without any search**, so the engine
returns an arbitrary first move instead of playing the position.

## The three-angle bound (the form for the FINAL)

> **Below counter 100 it cannot fire. At 100 and above it always fires, and the substitute move is not merely
> unscored — it is wrong. On PC r15 it never fires, under either settings regime.**

## 1. Threshold: exactly counter 100 (19-C37)

Mate-in-1 board `6k1/5ppp/8/8/8/8/5PPP/R5K1 w`, `go depth 12`, Threads 1, OwnBook false:

| counter | base 6b98f217 | PC r15 |
|---|---|---|
| 0, 50, 98, **99** | 252 nodes, **`mate 1`**, `a1a8` | 252 nodes, `mate 1`, `a1a8` |
| **100**, 101, 150, **9999** | **0 nodes, `cp 0`, `f2f3`** | 252 nodes, `mate 1`, `a1a8` |

**The 99 → 100 step is the cleanest demonstration:** one half-move of counter turns a *found mate* into a
*fabricated quiet move*. Testing at **9,999** as well as 100/101 is what makes "every counter at or above 100"
solid rather than extrapolated. This confirms seat 21's 21-F9 threshold claim exactly.

send avoids it on the base build.**

**19-F10 — software prefetching the NNUE weight columns makes the engine 8 % SLOWER.**
Adding `_mm_prefetch` for the next 16-float block of each of the (up to six) weight columns in
`nnue::fuse_columns` / `nnue::update` costs 8.10 % of nps (95 % CI [-11.59 %, -4.48 %], 20 pairs), with all

| node ratio (PC20/S14) | **0.9090 → 12.39 % fewer nodes** |
| engine-reported time ratio | **0.9728**, CI [0.9014, 1.0497] |
| external wall time (incl. startup) | 1.0070, CI [0.9622, 1.0539] |

**The node saving does NOT transfer proportionally.** PC20 is ~2.8 % faster, not ~12 %.

## Why — measured, not inferred
Two noisy ratios implied a per-node cost of ~1.066, but that is an inference. So I measured it directly at a
**fixed node budget**, where equal nodes make the time ratio *equal* the per-node cost:

| | S14 | PC20 | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| node totals | 6,721,052 | 6,591,407 | 0.9807 (budget-matched) |
| ms per 1M nodes | 51.66 | 55.24 | **1.0693** |
| per-position ln-ratio | | | **1.0773, CI [1.0670, 1.0876]** |

**PC20 costs ~7 % MORE per node on real positions.** (My first attempt at this used 4 positions and gave 1.0089 —
pure small-sample noise, and exactly the error this thread has been about. n = 180 settles it.)

**The reconciliation closes exactly:**
**0.9090 (nodes) × 1.0693 (per node) = 0.9720 predicted time ratio** vs **0.9728 observed.** Two independent
measurements, agreeing to 0.1 %.

## This qualifies my own 19-C35 — and I need to say so plainly

**19-C35 measured per-node cost on `bench 16` and reported 1.0119, CI [0.9997, 1.0241], concluding "at most ~1.2 %
slower". That interval does NOT overlap 1.0773 [1.0670, 1.0876].**

**`bench` is not a representative workload for per-node cost.** It replays a fixed position sequence with its own
`Searcher(16)` and a specific move mix; PC20's extra per-node work (`CuckooRep` maintenance, `HistRework` blending,
`TtPruneV2`/`CorrHistV2` probes) is exercised at a different rate there than on real game positions. **So 19-C35's
number was correct for bench and wrong as a general claim about PC20**, and I published it as the latter.

**Corrected statement:** *PC20 costs ~7 % more per node on real positions (1.0693, CI [1.0670, 1.0876], n=180)
while searching ~12 % fewer nodes at fixed depth; the net wall-time gain is ~2.8 %. On `bench` the per-node
penalty is only ~1.2 %, which is why bench-based reasoning overstated the speed win.*

## Also: a fixed-overhead test that pointed the wrong way, kept in the record
I tested whether the excess was a **fixed per-search cost** (which would amortise as the search grew) by measuring
the per-node ratio at budgets 2,000 / 5,000 / 20,000 / 100,000. **The ratio ROSE with budget (1.038 → 1.083), the
opposite of a fixed overhead**, which is consistent with a genuine per-node penalty that compounds. That is the
outcome that led me to the direct fixed-node measurement above. Recorded because the first hypothesis was wrong
and the test is what corrected it.

## For the owner, in one line
**PC20 at fixed depth is about 2.8 % faster in wall time, not the 12 % its node count suggests** — because it pays
~7 % per node. At matched *nodes* (his match condition) that means **an S14-vs-PC20 match at equal nodes is not an
equal-time match: PC20 spends ~7 % more time to reach the same node count.** That is a real, quantified cost of
the switches, and it is the number to weigh against PC20's depth advantage at 8k–20k.

# 19-C61 — PC20's net wall-time gain is NOT ESTABLISHED at n=464. My prediction failed, and the node saving shrank.

## Why this run existed

19-C53 reported pooled time ratio 0.9343, **CI [0.8676, 1.0082]**, which **includes 1.0** — so "PC20 is ~2.8 %
faster" was not supported. Rather than leave it open I quadrupled the sample: **470 positions, 464 usable**.

**My prediction, committed in STATUS before the run:** the CI would narrow by ~√(470/119) ≈ 2× to about ±4 %, and
if the true ratio were 0.93–0.94 it would then **exclude 1.0**.

## Result — the prediction failed
**Pooled time ratio 0.9715, bootstrap 95 % CI [0.9273, 1.0151]. It still includes 1.0.**

| | n = 119 | **n = 464** |
|---|---|---|
| pooled **time** ratio | 0.9343 [0.8676, 1.0082] | **0.9715 [0.9273, 1.0151]** |
| pooled **node** ratio | 0.8761 [0.8196, 0.9364] | **0.9131 [0.8752, 0.9528]** |
| node sign-share | 60.5 % | **59.9 %** (278/464) |
| time sign-share | 52.9 % | **50.9 %** (236/464) |
| node saving | 12.39 % | **8.69 %** |

**Two things happened, and the first is the important one: the effect shrank as the sample grew.**
The node saving went **12.39 % → 8.69 %**, and the time ratio moved **toward 1.0** (0.9343 → 0.9715). The point
estimate was not stable across sample sizes; it drifted in the direction of *less* effect. This is the same
pattern 29-N42 documented for its own work ("every magnitude of mine shrank as samples grew").

**Second: the time CI still straddles 1.0 at n=464.** With 464 pairs and a 2.0× reduction in CI width, a true 7 %
speedup would have been detected. **It was not. So PC20's net wall-time advantage is not established at this scale,
and I am not going to keep widening the sample to chase it.**

## What *is* established, and it reproduces independently
| claim | pooled | CI | sign-share | class |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PC20 uses **fewer nodes** | 0.9131 (−8.69 %) | **[0.8752, 0.9528] excludes 1.0** | 59.9 % | **REAL, session-level** |
| PC20 is **faster in wall time** | 0.9715 (−2.85 %) | [0.9273, 1.0151] includes 1.0 | 50.9 % | **NOT ESTABLISHED** |
| **per-node cost** (implied) | **1.0640** | — | — | **REAL** |

**The per-node figure reproduces from a completely different calculation:** implied time/node at n=464 = **1.0640**,
against the direct fixed-node measurement of **1.0693** at n=180 (19-C53b). **Two methods, two sample sizes, 0.5 %
apart.** That is the strongest internal consistency in this whole thread, and it means the per-node tax is the solid
result while the net speed is the fragile one.

## The corrected owner statement
**PC20 searches ~9 % fewer nodes (real, but only ~60 % of positions) and pays ~6.4 % more per node (real, uniform).
Those two nearly cancel: the net wall-time difference is −2.9 % with a CI that includes zero, so it is NOT
established.** Anyone quoting a "PC20 speedup" should quote the node saving and the per-node cost separately and say
the net is unmeasured — which is exactly what the node saving does *not* deliver on its own.

## Lesson
**A point estimate that drifts toward 1.0 as n grows, while its CI narrows past the effect, is a small-sample
artefact being corrected in public.** 19-C53's 0.9343 was not wrong as a measurement — it was a n=119 estimate of an
effect that is smaller than n=119 could resolve. **The failure was mine in reporting a point estimate ("~2.8 %
faster") from an interval that included 1.0**, which is the same error the CI-first rule now forbids.

non-search as the deepest thing it had seen.

## Build note worth writing down

The box's default `c++` cannot link — `cannot find -lstdc++`. Every configure attempt fails at the
compiler probe unless **`-DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=g++-13` is named explicitly**. I lost two builds to
this before noticing, and the second failure was worse than the first: a rebuild that reused a stale
`CMakeCache.txt` from a copied tree produced a binary **byte-identical** to the old one while
reporting `[100%] Built target forge` and `EXIT=0`. That is the header's own rule firing on me —
**the treatment was not applied** — and the tell was again an exact sha256 match.

## The rule

**A patch that fixes a symptom can reproduce the symptom's essence in reduced form.** v1's "1 line
instead of 64" was a real improvement and still asserted a completed depth in 0 nodes. When the
complaint is *"this number is a lie"*, the fix has to make the number true, not just make it rarer.
Check the surviving line's content, not only its count.

## A unit error of mine that took four attempts, recorded

My mate-distance solver disagreed with itself across three versions because I mixed **plies** and **moves**:
UCI's `score mate K` counts MOVES, so `mate 2` is 3 plies. My first versions returned ply counts and I then
compared them against ply-based and move-based checks in turn, "fixing" a solver that was sometimes right.
The version shipped returns MOVES (`2d−1` plies for distance `d`) and is asserted against the board above,
whose distance six independent wins establish.

I also **dropped a board I had labelled mate-in-3**, because the solver said 2 and the solver was right —
the assertion caught my label, which is exactly what it is for. That is why this job reports mate-1 and
mate-2 cases and **no mate-3 case**: I could not produce a verified mate-in-3 board in the time, and I
would rather ship two proved cases than three where one is guessed.

- Whether `MateAlphaGuard true` (part of PC20) is what suppresses the mate score here. I did not run the

## What I am NOT sure about

- Whether the owner's match program would ever present a mate-in-2 at a drawn root. It is rare; the value

`runner.py` is written from the brief, not adapted from theirs. Hard-won details, each measured
(`FACTS_job2.md`): one bestmove per go (so i-th bestmove <-> i-th go, FIFO, and a mismatch voids the

hang detector that took its output mark AFTER writing `isready` (this produced 11 phantom "hangs" in my
first run) and a board tracker that ignored the `ucinewgame` reset (this produced 288 phantom "illegal
bestmoves"). Both phantom classes are gone in the two final runs: 0 hangs, 0 illegal.

### HEADLINE — the per-node price of MultiPV, and the one-line repair that removes it

At **MultiPV 1** the per-node cost is **FLAT at 0.8 microseconds at every Hash size**. At **MultiPV 3**
it climbs with the table and reaches **203.9 us/node** on a 2 GB hash (366 us on a second position) —
**for a byte-identical search tree**. Cause: `src/search.cpp:2879` calls `alt_shared->tt.clear()`
inside the per-PV-line loop opened at `:2851`, so the **whole table is zeroed once per extra line per
depth**, and `TranspositionTable::clear()` walks every cluster. Proof: wall time per clear is
**95–141 ms across eight cells** (MultiPV 2/3 x depths 6/8/10/12), independent of depth and line
count — what a full-table zeroing predicts and a search-side slowdown cannot.

| `go depth 8`, Threads 1, same 16,642 nodes | Hash 16 | 64 | 256 | 1024 | 2048 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MultiPV 3 — us/node | 2.0 | 4.7 | 17.2 | 117.5 | **203.9** |
| MultiPV 1 — us/node | 0.8 | 0.8 | 0.8 | 0.8 | 0.8 |

**THE DESIGN NOTE (the actionable repair, as measured — not the one-liner, which I ruled out).**
Stop the MultiPV loop calling `clear()` at all, and let each alternative line keep its own table
handle: the alternative lines **already own a separate table** (`alt_shared = make_unique<SharedSearchState>(hash_mb)` at `src/search.cpp:2730`), and every search already calls `tt.new_search()`,
which bumps the generation. The per-line `clear()` is therefore redundant full-table work. I built
exactly that — delete the single statement at `:2879` — and it **keeps all four honesty pins**
(312866 / 862329 / 3024920 / 4865609) while making the same eight cells **2.0x–4.2x faster**
(MultiPV 3, depth 12: 2,274.4 ms → 542.6 ms; the per-depth growth is gone, flat ~400–540 ms), and
MultiPV still returns **three distinct, legal lines** (the `search_moves` narrowing at `:2871` is what
keeps them distinct, not the clear). Patch: `check6/ttclear_no_alt_clear.patch.txt`.
**The one-line alternative I rejected:** replacing `clear()`'s body with a generation bump is
2.1x–4.9x faster but moves **bench 16 to 3,030,186** (+5,266 nodes) — a generation bump makes entries
*old*, not *unprobeable*, which a 5-bit generation cannot express; recorded as an experiment, not a
repair (`30-C29`, `30-C30`).

### 15-F5 — a terminal root is searched to depth 64 instead of answered at once (NEW)

```bash
cd forge-combo29/swarm/15/job3
grep -c "^info depth" evidence/asan/asan_000_nodes100.txt     # 64
grep -c "^info depth" evidence/asan/asan_000_depth5.txt       # 5
```

Raw line, from `evidence/asan/asan_000_depth5.txt` (FEN `7K/8/7q/8/8/8/bk4r1/8 w`, white mated):

```
info depth 5 seldepth 5 score mate 0 nodes 0 nps 0 hashfull 0 time 0 pv
bestmove 0000
```

Two separate defects in one behaviour:

1. **The score type is wrong.** At a checkmated root the score is printed as `score mate 0`.
   UCI reserves `mate 0` for nothing; a mate **score** of 0 with the side to move checkmated
   should not be emitted as a mate score at all. On a stalemated root the same position prints
   `score cp 0`, so the two terminal cases are reported inconsistently.
2. **The iteration is not terminated.** With `go nodes 100`, `go movetime 50` and `go depth 64`
   the engine emits 64 info lines with `nodes 0` and `time 0..4`, i.e. it walks the depth ladder
   to the clamp maximum although there is no move to search. With `go depth D` it emits exactly
   D lines, so the ladder is driven by the limit, not by anything about the position.

Reproduces on the release build as well, so it is not a sanitizer artefact:

```
depth 5      info_lines=5    last: info depth 5 seldepth 5 score cp 0 nodes 0 ... pv   bestmove 0000
nodes 100    info_lines=64   last: info depth 64 seldepth 64 score cp 0 nodes 0 ... pv  bestmove 0000
movetime 50  info_lines=64   last: info depth 64 seldepth 64 score cp 0 nodes 0 ... pv  bestmove 0000
```

**Impact.** Small in time (the whole walk is ~20-30 ms wall) but it is 64 spurious lines on every
terminal position, and any GUI or test harness that decides "the engine searched" by the presence
of an `info depth` line will mis-read a dead position as a searched one — which is exactly the trap
that cost 80 rows in my own job 2 analysis (`15-F4`).

## Suspicions, not proven

- The `nodes 0` with a rising `seldepth` in the same line suggests the seldepth counter is being
  incremented per iteration without any node being visited; I did not read the code to confirm.
- `score mate 0` may be the engine's internal "mated now" encoding leaking into the UCI writer
  without a special case. Not established.

## What I did NOT do

- Did not read the search or UCI source to find the cause (area 7's job).
- Did not test positions where a side is mated *in one* (i.e. non-terminal roots with mate 0) —
  only true terminal roots.
- Did not run TSan on this job; area 4 owns threads.
- Did not measure how the 64-line walk behaves at Threads > 1.

## What I am NOT sure about

- Whether a GUIs cares about the 64 lines in practice; I only assert the files show it.
- Whether `mate 0` is intended as "no mate" for some downstream consumer. I state only that it is
  not a legal UCI mate score and that it is inconsistent with the stalemate case printing cp 0.
